reason: The cited evidence (E1, E2) shows that in ultra-high vacuum (without oxidation) CoCrFeMnNi forms a nanocrystalline layer giving friction ~0.3 and low wear, and notes that in oxygen environments HEAs form oxide films that reduce wear. However, the evidence does not demonstrate that a controlled oxidation treatment produces a spinel-type film, nor that such a film reduces friction to below 0.1 or remains stable up to 800°C. The key premises about the specific oxide phase, its friction reduction magnitude, and high-temperature stability are unsupported by the cited passages.
premises: CoCrFeMnNi can form an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer during sliding in inert environments, linked to low friction (~0.3) and low wear (~10^-6 mm^3/N-m).
In oxygen-containing environments, HEAs generally form mixed metal-oxide films that reduce wear rate and increase hardness.
A controlled oxidation treatment can produce a stable, adherent, spinel-type nanocrystalline oxide film on CoCrFeMnNi.
This oxide film will act as a self-adaptive tribolayer, reducing friction coefficient from ~0.3 to below 0.1 and wear rate by at least one order of magnitude.
The oxide film will remain effective and adherent from room temperature up to ~800°C under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading.
